posts.title: Countries With No Minimum Stay Residency: The Complete List
posts.excerpt: Complete list of countries with no minimum stay residency requirements: Paraguay, Panama, UAE, Thailand Elite, and Nicaragua. Compare physical presence rules, costs, tax treatment, and citizenship potential. Paraguay wins on all fronts.
posts.author: Nexa Paraguay
posts.content:
## The Dream: Residency Without Living There

Most countries require you to spend 183+ days per year within their borders to maintain residency. This is the "physical presence trap" — you gain residency on paper, but you're locked into living there full-time.

For digital nomads, investors, retirees, and anyone with a global lifestyle, this defeats the purpose. You want the benefits of residency (tax optimization, legal status, a second home) without being chained to one location.

A small group of countries offers something different: **residency with no minimum stay requirement.**

Here's the complete list in 2026.

## The Complete List

| Country | Minimum Stay | Residency Type | Tax on Foreign Income | Citizenship Path | Setup Cost |
|---------|-------------|----------------|----------------------|-----------------|------------|
| **Paraguay** | **1 visit every 3 years** | Permanent Residency | **0%** | **3 years** | **$2,900+** |
| Panama | 1 day every 2 years | Permanent Residency (Friendly Nations) | 0% | 5-8 years | $5,000-8,000+ |
| UAE | 0 days (renew visa remotely) | Residence Visa (renewable) | 0% | No path | $5,000-10,000+ |
| Thailand Elite | 0 days (renew annually) | Privilege Visa (5-20 years) | 0% (foreign income) | No path | $15,000-60,000+ |
| Nicaragua | 1 visit every 2 years | Permanent Residency (investment) | 0% (territorial) | 4 years | $10,000+ |

## 1. Paraguay — The Overwhelming Winner

**Physical presence:** One visit every 3 years to renew your physical cédula. That's it. You can spend one afternoon at the migration office and leave the same day.

**Why it wins:**

- **Lowest physical presence requirement** — Every 3 years, not 2. And you don't need to stay overnight.
- **Cheapest setup** — $2,900+ all-in (lawyer fees, document apostilles, migration fees, cédula costs).
- **Best tax treatment** — 0% on all foreign income. No wealth tax. No capital gains tax on foreign assets.
- **Only country with a citizenship path** — After 3 years of permanent residency, you can apply for citizenship. None of the other "no stay" options offer this.
- **No income requirement** — Qualify on savings alone. No minimum monthly income.
- **No CRS reporting** — Paraguay doesn't share financial data with other countries.
- **Crypto-friendly** — Crypto treated as goods, 0% capital gains tax, no DAC8 reporting.

**Who it's for:** Digital nomads, remote workers, retirees, investors, crypto holders, anyone wanting a second passport.

### How It Works

1. Enter Paraguay as a tourist.
2. Your lawyer files your residency application.
3. You visit the migration office (one appointment, ~30 minutes).
4. 60-90 days later, you get your cédula (permanent residency ID).
5. Return every 3 years for a 15-minute renewal.

**That's it.** No annual renewals. No income reporting. No tax filings on foreign income.

## 2. Panama — The Runner-Up

**Physical presence:** 1 day every 2 years.

Panama's Friendly Nations Visa offers permanent residency with a minimal stay requirement. You must visit Panama once every two years to maintain your residency.

**Pros:** 0% foreign income tax, US dollar economy, strong banking, good infrastructure.

**Cons:** Higher cost ($5,000-8,000+ setup), citizenship takes 5-8 years, requires a job offer or investment for most visa categories, higher cost of living ($1,200-1,800/mo).

Panama is a strong alternative, especially for those who want proximity to North America and a more developed infrastructure. But it's more expensive upfront and takes longer for citizenship.

## 3. UAE — Zero Days, Zero Future

**Physical presence:** Can be maintained entirely remotely. No minimum stay.

The UAE offers residence visas (usually 2-3 years, renewable) tied to employment, freelancing (freelance visa), property ownership, or investment. No physical presence required.

**Pros:** True 0% tax on all income, world-class infrastructure, Dubai lifestyle, no CRS reporting.

**Cons:** Citizenship is virtually impossible regardless of how long you stay. The "residency" is a renewable visa, not permanent status. High cost of living ($1,800-3,000+). Visas require ongoing financial commitments (e.g., property, employment, or bank deposits).

The UAE works well for high earners who want zero tax and don't care about a second passport. For everyone else, it's expensive and has no exit strategy.

## 4. Thailand Elite — Expensive and Temporary

**Physical presence:** 0 days. Visa can be maintained remotely.

The Thailand Elite Visa is a program that grants long-term stays (5, 10, or 20 years) in exchange for a lump-sum fee. No physical presence requirement.

**Pros:** No physical presence, no income tax on foreign income if not remitted, good lifestyle, easy application.

**Cons:** No path to citizenship. The fee ranges from $15,000 (5 years) to $60,000+ (20 years). You're still a temporary resident. Thailand tax laws can be tricky — remitted foreign income may be taxable. Visa is tied to the program, not genuine residency.

## 5. Nicaragua — The Dark Horse

**Physical presence:** 1 visit every 2 years.

Nicaragua offers permanent residency through investment (typically $30,000+ in real estate or a business). Physical presence is minimal — one visit every two years.

**Pros:** 0% tax on foreign income (territorial system), low cost of living ($500-800/mo), citizenship in 4 years.

**Cons:** Political instability, limited healthcare infrastructure, lower internet quality, fewer expat services. Setup costs around $10,000+ depending on investment.

Nicaragua is worth considering for those on a tight budget, but the political and infrastructure risks are real.

## Detailed Comparison: Paraguay vs. the Field

### Citizenship Path

This is the single biggest differentiator.

| Country | Time to Citizenship | Dual Citizenship Allowed? |
|---------|-------------------|--------------------------|
| **Paraguay** | **3 years** | **Yes** |
| Panama | 5-8 years | Yes (limited) |
| UAE | No path | N/A |
| Thailand Elite | No path | N/A |
| Nicaragua | 4 years | Yes |

Only Paraguay and Nicaragua offer a real citizenship path. Paraguay does it faster, cheaper, and with less risk.

### Tax Comparison

| Country | Foreign Income Tax | Capital Gains Tax | Wealth Tax | CRS |
|---------|-------------------|-------------------|------------|-----|
| **Paraguay** | **0%** | **0% (foreign)** | **0%** | **No** |
| Panama | 0% | 0% (foreign) | 0% | No |
| UAE | 0% | 0% | 0% | No |
| Thailand Elite | 0% (if not remitted) | 0% (foreign) | 0% | No |
| Nicaragua | 0% | 0% (foreign) | 0% | No |

All five countries are tax-competitive. Paraguay's advantage is that it's the clearest and most established territorial tax system.

### Cost Comparison

| Country | Setup Cost | Monthly COL (single) | Total First Year |
|---------|-----------|---------------------|------------------|
| **Paraguay** | **$2,900** | **$700-1,100** | **$11,200-16,100** |
| Panama | $5,000-8,000 | $1,200-1,800 | $19,400-29,600 |
| UAE | $5,000-10,000+ | $1,800-3,000 | $26,600-46,000+ |
| Thailand Elite | $15,000-60,000 | $800-1,500 | $24,600-78,000+ |
| Nicaragua | $10,000+ | $500-800 | $16,000-19,600+ |

Paraguay is both the cheapest to set up and one of the cheapest to maintain.

## The Fine Print

### What "No Minimum Stay" Really Means

Every country on this list requires some form of ongoing connection. For Paraguay, it's a 15-minute cédula renewal every 3 years. For Panama, it's a quick visit every 2 years. For Thailand Elite, it's an annual renewal fee.

None of these require you to "live" there. You can spend 364 days a year anywhere else in the world.

### What Could Go Wrong

- **Policy changes** — Any country can change its rules. Paraguay's immigration framework is established in law (not a temporary program), making it more stable.
- **Tax residency audit** — If you spend 183+ days in another country, that country may claim you as a tax resident. Paraguay's 0-day requirement protects you from this.
- **Renewal complications** — Some countries make renewals bureaucratic. Paraguay's cédula renewal is straightforward — pay a fee, update fingerprints, done.

## The Bottom Line

If you want residency without living there, you have five real options:

| If you want... | Go with... |
|----------------|-----------|
| Lowest cost + best value | **Paraguay** |
| Fastest citizenship | **Paraguay** (3 years) |
| Best infrastructure | UAE (but no passport) |
| North America proximity | Panama |
| Cheapest monthly | Nicaragua (but risky) |
| Guaranteed long-term without residency | Thailand Elite |

**Paraguay is the only country that gives you no minimum stay, permanent residency from day one, 0% tax on foreign income, and a path to citizenship in 3 years — all for under $3,000 setup cost.**

No other country on this list can say that.

---

## The 0% Crypto Tax Club: Who Qualifies and How to Join

Crypto investors face a rapidly closing window in most developed countries. With DAC8 going live across the EU, the ATO in Australia pursuing wallet-level enforcement, and countries like Italy hiking crypto taxes to 33%, the search for tax-efficient jurisdictions has never been more urgent.

Seven countries still charge 0% capital gains tax on cryptocurrency. But not all 0% jurisdictions are equal. Here's the definitive comparison for 2026.

| **Paraguay** | **0%** | Low ($2,900+) | Yes (3 yrs) | No | $1,200-$2,000 |
| UAE | 0% | High ($544k prop. or $136k salary) | No | Partial | $2,500-$5,000 |

| Cayman Islands | 0% | High ($2M+ invest.) | No | No | $3,000-$6,000 |
| BVI | 0% | High ($100k+ fees) | No | No | $2,500-$5,000 |
| Bahamas | 0% | High ($750k prop.) | Yes (8-12 yrs) | No | $2,500-$4,500 |
| Bermuda | 0% | High ($2.5M invest.) | No | Partial | $4,000-$7,000 |

## 1. Paraguay — The Clear Winner

**Cryptocurrency tax rate: 0% on foreign-source gains**

Paraguay stands alone as the most accessible, affordable, and strategically advantageous jurisdiction for crypto investors.

### Why Paraguay Wins

- **Foreign crypto gains: 0% tax** — Paraguay's territorial system doesn't tax income earned outside its borders
- **No wealth tax, no inheritance tax, no estate tax**
- **Not a CRS participant** — your crypto holdings stay private from your home country
- **Residency from $2,900+** — no minimum investment required
- **Citizenship in 3 years** — one of the fastest programs globally
- **No minimum physical presence** — visit once every 3 years to maintain residency
- **Internet 50-300 Mbps** — fiber in Asuncion and Ciudad del Este
- **Cost of living: $1,200-$2,000/month** — a fraction of other 0% jurisdictions

### Crypto Infrastructure

- **X4T** — Paraguay's first government-licensed crypto exchange, bank-integrated
- **Ueno** — crypto-friendly digital bank with fiat on/off ramps
- **Oobit** — spend crypto via card accepted at 100M+ merchants
- **Schwab International** — US brokerage available to PY residents

### DNIT Resolution 47/2026

Paraguay introduced crypto reporting obligations in March 2026. But critically: this is AML/KYC reporting, not a tax. You must declare crypto holdings above $5,000 in annual transactions, but you pay 0% tax on foreign gains. It's a compliance requirement, not a tax imposition.

## 2. UAE — The Luxury Option

**Cryptocurrency tax rate: 0%**

The UAE offers 0% personal income tax and 0% capital gains tax. Dubai in particular has built a thriving crypto ecosystem with the VARA regulator and Dubai Multi Commodities Centre (DMCC) Crypto Valley.

### Downsides

- **Residency requires either a $544,000 property purchase or a $2,720/month salary** with employer sponsorship
- **No path to citizenship** — naturalization is not available for foreigners
- **High cost of living** — $2,500-$5,000/month minimum
- **CRS reporting applies** to UAE financial accounts for residents from most countries
- **The "economic substance" requirements** are tightening yearly
- **Extreme summer heat** — not for everyone

Best for: High-net-worth investors who can afford $500K+ property and want luxury lifestyle alongside zero tax.

## 3. Qatar — Oil Wealth, Limited Access

**Cryptocurrency tax rate: 0%** (no personal income tax)

Qatar has no personal income tax, meaning 0% on crypto gains. The Qatar Financial Centre (QFC) has also been developing digital asset frameworks.

### Downsides

- **Employer sponsorship required** for residency — no independent investor visa
- **No path to citizenship**
- **Crypto ecosystem is underdeveloped** compared to UAE or Paraguay
- **CRS reporting applies**
- **High cost of living** and strict social norms

## 4. Cayman Islands — Zero Tax, High Entry

**Cryptocurrency tax rate: 0%**

The Cayman Islands has no direct taxation at all — no income tax, no capital gains tax, no corporate tax, no withholding tax.

### Downsides

- **Residency requires a $2M+ investment** or significant economic substance
- **No citizenship path** (permanent residency possible after 6+ years)
- **Extremely high cost of living** — $3,000-$6,000/month
- **Banking is difficult** for crypto-exposed clients
- **Global tax crackdown** — OECD scrutiny is intense
- **Hurricane risk**

## 5. BVI — Corporate Structure, Not Personal

**Cryptocurrency tax rate: 0%** (no direct taxes)

The British Virgin Islands has no capital gains, income, or corporate taxes. Ideal for corporate structures.

### Downsides

- **Individual residency requires $100,000+ in professional fees** and government charges
- **No citizenship path**
- **Very small population and limited lifestyle options**
- **Intense OECD/UK scrutiny** — BVI is on multiple grey lists
- **Banking is extremely difficult** — many banks refuse BVI entities

## 6. Bahamas — Tax-Free, Slow Citizenship

**Cryptocurrency tax rate: 0%**

The Bahamas has no income tax, no capital gains tax, no corporate tax. The "Bahamas Blockchain" initiative has attracted some crypto business.

### Downsides

- **Residency by investment requires $750,000** in real estate
- **Citizenship possible but takes 8-12 years**
- **Cost of living: $2,500-$4,500/month**
- **Hurricane risk and geographic isolation**
- **Smaller crypto ecosystem**

## 7. Bermuda — Premium Price Tag

**Cryptocurrency tax rate: 0%**

Bermuda has the most developed regulatory framework for digital assets among the islands, with the Bermuda Monetary Authority offering licensing for crypto businesses.

### Downsides

- **Investment requirement of $2.5M+** for residency
- **No citizenship path**
- **Highest cost of living on this list** — $4,000-$7,000/month
- **CRS reporting applies**
- **Very strict banking regulations**

## The Verdict: Paraguay Wins on All Practical Metrics

| Factor | Paraguay | UAE | Qatar | Cayman | BVI | Bahamas | Bermuda |
|--------|----------|-----|-------|--------|-----|---------|---------|
| **Entry Cost** | $2,900+ | $136k+ | Sponsored | $2M+ | $100k+ | $750k+ | $2.5M+ |
| **Citizenship** | 3 years | No | No | No | No | 8-12 yrs | No |
| **CRS** | No | Yes | Yes | No | No | No | Yes |
| **Monthly Cost** | $1,200-$2k | $2.5k-$5k | $2k-$4k | $3k-$6k | $2.5k-$5k | $2.5k-$4.5k | $4k-$7k |
| **Physical Presence** | 0 days/yr | None | Full-time | None | None | None | None |
| **Crypto Ecosystem** | Growing | Mature | Early | Early | Small | Early | Regulated |
| **Banking Access** | Good | Excellent | Limited | Difficult | Difficult | Good | Difficult |

## The Bottom Line

If you have $2 million to invest and want zero taxes, the Cayman Islands works. If you want a luxury desert lifestyle and have half a million for property, the UAE is great. But if you want the best balance of zero crypto taxes, affordable entry, a real citizenship path, and the freedom to live anywhere — Paraguay is the only country that delivers on all fronts.

The 0% crypto tax club is shrinking, not growing. As DAC8, CARF, and OECD pressure mount, jurisdictions without solid legal foundations are caving. Paraguay's territorial tax system, however, is constitutional and has been stable for decades. It's not a loophole. It's the law.

posts.title: Crypto-Friendly Banking in Paraguay: X4T, Ueno, Oobit & More
posts.excerpt: Paraguay's crypto banking ecosystem is growing fast. X4T is the country's first licensed crypto exchange with bank integration. Ueno offers a crypto-friendly digital bank. Oobit enables spending crypto anywhere. Plus Schwab International and Itaú for traditional banking.
posts.author: Nexa Paraguay
posts.content:
## The Crypto Banking Landscape in Paraguay

One of the biggest concerns for crypto investors relocating is banking access. Can you open a bank account? Can you move between crypto and fiat easily? Will the bank freeze your funds if they see exchange transfers?

In Paraguay, the answer is increasingly yes — as long as you know the right platforms.

## X4T: Paraguay's First Licensed Crypto Exchange

X4T launched in December 2021 as Paraguay's first government-licensed cryptocurrency exchange. It has since become the largest and most trusted platform in the country.

### What Makes X4T Different

**Licensed and Regulated**
X4T operates under full regulatory oversight in Paraguay. Unlike offshore exchanges that operate in grey areas, X4T is fully compliant with local law, including DNIT Resolution 47/2026 reporting requirements. This means:

- Your funds are held by a regulated entity
- Bank integrations are legally structured
- No sudden "unsupported jurisdiction" messages
- Full audit trail for your tax filings

**Bank Integration**
X4T allows you to buy and sell crypto directly via bank transfer to Paraguayan bank accounts (Ueno, Itaú, and others). You can:

- Deposit guaranis via bank transfer
- Buy USDT, BTC, ETH, and major altcoins
- Sell back to fiat and withdraw to your local bank account
- Use the mobile app for on-the-go trading

**Zero Trading Fees**
X4T charges 0% trading fees — significantly cheaper than Binance, Kraken, or Coinbase.

**Dollar Accounts**
X4T offers dollar-denominated account options, allowing you to hold USD alongside your crypto, reducing FX exposure.

### How to Get Started with X4T

1. Download the app (iOS and Android)
2. Complete KYC verification (passport, proof of address, source of funds)
3. Fund your account via bank transfer from your Paraguayan bank
4. Start trading — 0% fees, instant execution

## Ueno: Crypto-Friendly Digital Banking

Ueno is a Paraguayan digital bank that has positioned itself as the most crypto-friendly banking option in the country.

### Key Features

- **SEPA-compatible** — can receive EUR transfers from Europe
- **SWIFT international transfers** — move money from your home country
- **Integration with X4T** — seamless fiat-to-crypto transfers
- **US dollar accounts** — hold USD alongside PYG
- **Debit card** — spend from your account at any POS terminal
- **Mobile-first** — everything happens through the app

### Why Ueno Works for Crypto Investors

Ueno understands that crypto investors need to move between fiat and digital assets. Their onboarding process is straightforward, and they don't freeze accounts for legitimate exchange activity. However, you should still be prepared to explain your source of funds with proper documentation.

**Account Opening Requirements:**
- Valid passport
- Proof of Paraguayan address (can be a rental contract)
- Source of funds documentation
- Minimum deposit: typically none or very low

## Oobit: Spend Crypto Anywhere

Oobit is a crypto spending platform that works seamlessly in Paraguay. It provides a crypto card that converts your crypto to guaranis at the point of sale, allowing you to spend your digital assets anywhere.

### How Oobit Works

1. Connect your wallet (MetaMask, Binance, Trust Wallet)
2. Load USDT, BTC, or ETH
3. Pay with the Oobit card at any merchant
4. The merchant receives guaranis — they never touch crypto
5. You spend your crypto without triggering a taxable event (in Paraguay)

### Oobit in Paraguay

- Accepted at 100M+ merchants globally
- Works with Paraguay's POS network
- Supports USDT, BTC, ETH, and major stablecoins
- No need to sell crypto to fiat first
- Instant conversion at market rates

## Traditional Banks Accepting Crypto in Paraguay

### Schwab International

Charles Schwab International accounts are available to Paraguay residents. Schwab is among the most crypto-friendly traditional brokerages:

- High-yield checking account (typically 0.45%+ APY)
- No foreign transaction fees
- Unlimited ATM fee rebates globally
- Access to US stock market, bonds, ETFs
- No issue with transfers from crypto exchanges (within reason)

**Note:** Schwab is a US brokerage. Your accounts may be reportable under FATCA (US accounts held by foreign residents). But Schwab does not participate in CRS for non-US persons.

### Itaú Paraguay (Selective)

Itaú is one of Brazil's largest banks, and its Paraguayan branch offers some flexibility for crypto-adjacent clients. However, Itaú is more selective than Ueno or Schwab.

**Tips for Itaú:**
- Open the account first, then introduce crypto activity gradually
- Be transparent about your sources of wealth
- Expect to provide substantial documentation
- Relationship matters — work with a manager who understands crypto

### Other Options

- **Banco Continental** — accepts some crypto-adjacent clients
- **Banco Familiar** — more flexible, smaller bank
- **Vision Banco** — open to foreign residents with proper documentation

## The Complete Crypto-Financial Stack

For a crypto investor relocating to Paraguay, here's the recommended setup:

| Purpose | Provider | Why |
|---------|----------|-----|
| Daily banking | Ueno | Crypto-friendly, SWIFT, debit card |
| Crypto exchange | X4T | Licensed, 0% fees, bank-integrated |
| Crypto spending | Oobit | Spend directly without selling |
| US investments | Schwab International | Access to US markets, ATM rebates |
| Local backup | Itaú Paraguay | Traditional banking for larger sums |

## Getting Paraguayan Banking Right

The key to successful banking in Paraguay as a crypto investor is:

1. **Prepare documentation** — source of funds, tax returns, exchange statements
2. **Start simple** — open a basic account first, add complexity later
3. **Use proper channels** — X4T is regulated; avoid P2P cash exchanges
4. **Maintain records** — DNIT Res 47 requires annual reporting; good records make this easy
5. **Build relationships** — banking in Paraguay is relationship-driven; a good manager is worth gold

## The Bottom Line

Paraguay's banking ecosystem for crypto investors has matured significantly. With X4T as a licensed exchange, Ueno as a crypto-friendly bank, and Oobit for spending, you have a complete financial infrastructure. Add Schwab International and a local backup bank like Itaú, and you have everything you need to manage your crypto wealth from Paraguay — with 0% tax on foreign gains and no CRS reporting.

posts.title: Crypto Tax Exiles: Why European Investors Are Choosing Paraguay in 2026
posts.excerpt: With 49 million+ European crypto holders facing DAC8 reporting and tax rates from 28% to 36%+, Paraguay is the top destination for crypto tax exiles in 2026. Netherlands taxes unrealised gains at 36%, Germany up to 47.5% short-term, Spain 28%, Italy 33%. Paraguay: 0%.
posts.author: Nexa Paraguay
posts.content:
## The Great Crypto Migration Has Begun

Europe has 49 million cryptocurrency holders according to Triple-A's 2025 estimates. After January 1, 2026, every single one of them became visible to their local tax authority through DAC8. And for most, the tax bill is devastating.

The result? A wave of crypto tax exiles — investors who are restructuring their tax residence to jurisdictions that don't treat crypto gains as taxable events.

Paraguay has become the primary destination for these exiles, and for good reason.

## The European Tax Crisis for Crypto Holders

### Netherlands: The Unrealised Gains Trap

The Netherlands has implemented one of the most aggressive tax regimes in the world for crypto investors.

**Pre-2026:** Box 3 taxed deemed returns on a fictional 5.88% yield at 36% — whether you earned anything or not.

**2026 and beyond:** The new system taxes actual returns, including unrealised price appreciation, at 36%. If your Bitcoin goes up in value but you don't sell, you still owe 36% of that increase.

**Real-world impact:** A Dutch investor with €500,000 in crypto that appreciated by 20% (€100,000) owes €36,000 in tax — despite having sold nothing. This has effectively made crypto holding impossible for serious Dutch investors.

"*I moved to Paraguay because the Dutch government wanted to tax me on gains I hadn't even realized. My crypto portfolio was up €180,000 on paper, and my tax bill was €64,800. That's my children's inheritance they were taxing before I could even access it.*" — Mark, former Netherlands resident, now Paraguay cedula holder

### Germany: The End of the 1-Year Rule

Germany historically offered one of the best crypto tax regimes in Europe: hold for 1 year and sell tax-free. This is now under active threat.

**Current rules:**
- Short-term gains (<1 year): taxed at personal income tax rate up to 45% + 5.5% solidarity surcharge = up to 47.475%
- Long-term gains (>1 year): tax-free (currently)
- April 2026 legislative proposals to abolish the 1-year exemption

**The reality:** Even under current rules, a German day trader or DeFi user making €200,000 in short-term gains owes ~€95,000 to the tax authority. And if the 1-year exemption falls, long-term holders face the same rates.

"*Germany was great for crypto until you actually needed to trade. I couldn't use DeFi, couldn't arbitrage, couldn't do anything active without triggering massive tax bills. Paraguay gives me the freedom to actually use crypto the way it was meant to be used.*" — Klaus, former German resident

### Spain: 28% on Large Gains

Spain taxes crypto gains as savings income with progressive rates reaching 28% on gains over €300,000.

**The problem:** Spain's tax authorities (Agencia Tributaria) have become increasingly aggressive on crypto enforcement. DAC8 will give them full visibility into Spanish residents' foreign exchange accounts.

"*Spain was beautiful but expensive. I was paying €56,000 in crypto taxes and another €30,000+ in wealth taxes on my global assets. In Paraguay, that same portfolio generates exactly zero tax. I rent a beautiful apartment in Asuncion for €600/month and live like a king.*" — Carlos, former Spanish resident

### Italy: 33% Flat Rate

Italy raised its crypto capital gains tax from 26% to 33% effective January 1, 2026, and abolished the €2,000 exemption threshold.

**The math:** An Italian investor with €500,000 in crypto gains now owes €165,000 in tax. Years of crypto profits built through careful investing, taxed at one-third.

"*The 33% rate was the final straw. I had been thinking about leaving for years, but when they raised the rate and removed the exemption, I realized Italy would never be friendly to crypto wealth. I now live in Paraguay, pay 0% on my foreign crypto income, and I'm on track for citizenship in 3 years.*" — Marco, former Italian resident

## Why Paraguay — Not UAE, Not Portugal

### Portugal: The Fallen Star

Portugal was once the crypto tax haven of Europe. No tax on crypto gains for individuals. The Non-Habitual Resident (NHR) program offered 10-year tax holidays.

**What changed:**
- 2023: Portugal introduced a 28% tax on crypto held less than 365 days
- 2024: NHR program effectively ended for most new applicants
- 2026: Income tax brackets up to 48% apply to crypto trading income
- CRS reporting applies — your home country is notified

Portugal is no longer a viable option for crypto tax exiles. The 0% crypto tax era in Portugal is over.

### UAE: The Expensive Alternative

The UAE offers 0% personal tax, but:
- Requires $544K property or $136K salary for residency
- No path to citizenship
- CRS reporting for most residents
- $2,500+/month cost of living
- Economic substance requirements tightening

### Paraguay: The Clear Winner

| Factor | Paraguay | UAE | Portugal (2026) |
|--------|----------|-----|-------------------|
| **Crypto CGT** | 0% | 0% | Up to 48% |
| **Residency Cost** | $2,900+ | $136K+ | Low (visa) |
| **Citizenship** | 3 years | No | 5 years |
| **CRS** | No | Yes | Yes |
| **Monthly Living** | $1,200-$2k | $2.5k-$5k | $1.5k-$3k |
| **Physical Presence** | None | None | 183 days/yr |

## Case Study: From 36% to 0%

**Investor Profile:** Dutch, €2M crypto portfolio, €400K annual trading gains

**Netherlands Scenario (2026):**
- Box 3 tax on unrealised: ~€72,000 (36% of €200K paper gain)
- Actual trading gains: €400,000 x 36% = €144,000
- Wealth tax component on total assets
- **Total annual tax: ~€150,000+**

**Paraguay Scenario:**
- Foreign crypto gains: 0%
- Wealth tax: 0%
- VAT on local spending: 10%
- **Total annual tax: €0 on crypto**

The investor saves €150,000/year in taxes — enough to cover their entire cost of living in Paraguay multiple times over.

## Case Study: German DeFi User

**Investor Profile:** German, €500K crypto portfolio, active DeFi user, €150K annual yield

**Germany Scenario (2026):**
- Short-term staking/yield: ~€71,000 (47.5% top bracket)
- Every DeFi interaction creates a taxable event
- Administrative burden: tracking every transaction
- **Total annual tax: ~€71,000**

**Paraguay Scenario:**
- DeFi yield: 0% tax (foreign-source)
- No taxable events for intra-crypto trades
- Simple annual DNIT declaration
- **Total annual tax: €0**

## The Bottom Line

Europe's crypto tax landscape has shifted decisively against holders. DAC8 ensures compliance. Tax rates from 28% to 47%+ ensure the bill is painful. And countries like the Netherlands are even taxing unrealised gains — making it mathematically impossible to build long-term crypto wealth while residing there.

Paraguay offers a constitutional, stable, and proven alternative. 0% tax on foreign crypto gains. No CRS. Citizenship in 3 years. And a complete banking infrastructure with X4T, Ueno, and Oobit to manage your daily finances.

The question for European crypto investors isn't whether to leave. It's how fast you can get your cedula.

posts.title: DAC8 Crypto Reporting: What Changes January 2026 and What to Do About It
posts.excerpt: DAC8 takes effect January 1, 2026 — EU crypto platforms must report all user transactions to tax authorities. With NL taxing unrealized gains at 36%, DE at 26.375% short-term, ES at 28%, and IT at 33%, crypto investors face unprecedented scrutiny. Paraguay offers a 0% alternative.
posts.author: Nexa Paraguay
posts.content:
## DAC8 Is Live: What Crypto Investors Need to Know

On January 1, 2026, the European Union's DAC8 directive went into full effect. This is the most significant regulatory shift for crypto holders in EU history. Here's what changed, who it affects, and what you can do about it.

## What Is DAC8?

DAC8 (Directive on Administrative Cooperation, 8th iteration) requires all crypto-asset service providers — exchanges, brokers, wallet providers — operating in the EU to:

- **Collect detailed user data** including identity, residence, and transaction history
- **Report all crypto transactions** to national tax authorities automatically
- **Share data across EU member states** via automatic exchange of information

The first reporting deadline is September 2027 for the 2026 calendar year. But the data collection starts now.

## Country-by-Country Impact on Crypto Holders

### Netherlands: 36% Tax on Unrealised Gains

The Netherlands has taken the most aggressive stance. Under the reformed Box 3 system:

- **36% flat tax** on deemed returns from investments, including crypto
- **Tax applies even if you haven't sold** — unrealised gains are taxed
- **€57,000 exemption** per individual (€114,000 per couple)
- **Effective from 2026**, fully phased in by 2028

For a Dutch investor holding €500,000 in crypto that appreciated by 20% (€100,000), the tax bill is €36,000 — even if they never sold a single coin.

### Germany: 26.375% Short-Term (Plus Soli)

Germany's crypto tax regime:

- **Short-term gains** (held <1 year): taxed at your personal income tax rate, up to 45% plus 5.5% solidarity surcharge = **up to 47.475%**
- **The 1-year holding exemption is under threat** — as of April 2026, legislative changes are being debated to abolish it entirely
- **€600 annual exemption** for private sales
- **Cryptocurrency is classified as private assets**, not capital assets

A German trader making €100,000 in short-term crypto gains at the top bracket pays approximately €47,475 in tax.

### Spain: Up to 28% Capital Gains

Spain taxes crypto gains as savings income:

- **19% up to €6,000**
- **21% from €6,001 to €50,000**
- **23% from €50,001 to €200,000**
- **27% from €200,001 to €300,000**
- **28% over €300,000**

A Spanish investor with €500,000 in crypto gains faces €134,000+ in tax.

### Italy: 33% Flat Rate (Up from 26%)

Italy raised its crypto capital gains tax:

- **33% flat rate** from January 1, 2026 (up from 26%)
- **€2,000 exemption abolished** — all gains are now taxable
- **No distinction** between short-term and long-term holding

An Italian investor with €200,000 in crypto gains pays €66,000 in tax.

## The EU's Enforcement Arsenal

DAC8 isn't just a reporting requirement — it's an enforcement mechanism:

- **Automatic data exchange** between all 27 EU member states
- **Wallet-level reporting** for transactions over €1,000
- **DeFi and self-custody wallets NOT yet covered**, but the EU has signaled this is coming
- **Penalties for non-compliance** up to €5 million or 5% of annual turnover for platforms

## The Paraguay Solution: 0% on Foreign Crypto

While EU countries are racing to tax crypto gains more efficiently, Paraguay maintains a fundamentally different approach.

### Paraguay's Crypto Tax Treatment

| Aspect | Paraguay |
|--------|----------|
| **Foreign crypto gains** | 0% tax |
| **Capital gains tax** | 0% (foreign-source) |
| **Wealth tax** | 0% |
| **Inheritance tax** | 0% |
| **CRS reporting** | Not a participant |
| **DAC8** | Not applicable |
| **DNIT Res 47/2026** | Reporting only, not a tax |

### Why This Works

Paraguay operates a territorial tax system. Income sourced outside Paraguay — including crypto trades on foreign exchanges, DeFi yields, and NFT sales — is taxed at 0%. DNIT Resolution 47/2026 introduced reporting obligations in March 2026, but these are AML/KYC requirements, not a crypto tax. No capital gains tax, no wealth tax, no exit tax.

### The Numbers Don't Lie

Compare a €1,000,000 crypto portfolio across jurisdictions:

| Jurisdiction | Tax on €200k Gain | Effective Rate |
|-------------|------------------|----------------|
| Netherlands (Box 3) | €72,000 | 36% |
| Germany (short-term, top bracket) | ~€95,000 | ~47% |
| Spain (top bracket) | ~€56,000 | 28% |
| Italy (flat 33%) | €66,000 | 33% |
| **Paraguay** | **€0** | **0%** |

## What to Do If You're an EU Crypto Holder

### 1. Assess Your Exposure

Calculate what you'd owe under DAC8 reporting. Remember: tax authorities will have your data automatically starting with 2026 transactions.

### 2. Consider Relocation

Paraguay offers a clear path:

- **Permanent residency** in 3-6 months (traditional route, $2,900+)
- **Investor Pass** immediate permanent residency from $150,000 investment
- **Citizenship** after 3 years of residency
- **No minimum physical presence** required (visit every 3 years)

### 3. Plan Your Exit

EU exit tax rules vary by country. Some apply exit taxes on unrealised gains when you leave. Plan with a qualified advisor.

### 4. Use the Right Infrastructure

Once in Paraguay, you have access to:

- **X4T** — Paraguay's first licensed crypto exchange, bank-integrated
- **Ueno** — crypto-friendly digital bank
- **Oobit** — crypto spending card accepted locally and worldwide

## The Bottom Line

DAC8 is the beginning, not the end. With the EU pushing for wallet-level reporting, DeFi regulation, and higher crypto tax rates, the window for European crypto holders to restructure their tax residence is narrowing. Paraguay offers a proven, legal alternative with 0% tax on foreign crypto gains, no CRS reporting, and a fast path to a second passport.

The question isn't whether DAC8 will impact you. It's whether you'll act before the 2026 data starts flowing to your local tax authority.

posts.title: DNIT Resolution 47/2026: What Crypto Investors Must Report (And Why It's Not a Tax)
posts.excerpt: Paraguay's DNIT Resolution 47/2026 introduces mandatory crypto reporting — but it's AML/KYC compliance, not a crypto tax. No capital gains tax, no wealth tax, no income tax on foreign crypto. Compare with EU DAC8: same reporting, opposite tax outcome.
posts.author: Nexa Paraguay
posts.content:
## DNIT Resolution 47/2026: The Full Breakdown

In March 2026, Paraguay's National Directorate of Tax Revenue (DNIT) issued General Resolution No. 47/2026, introducing comprehensive reporting requirements for cryptocurrency transactions.

Headlines around the world screamed: "Paraguay Tightens Crypto Rules" and "New Crypto Tax in Paraguay."

The reality is far more nuanced — and far more favorable to crypto investors than the headlines suggest.

## What DNIT Resolution 47/2026 Actually Says

### The Legal Framework

Resolution 47/2026 is issued under the authority of Paraguay's tax code (Ley 125/91 and its modifications) and aligns with Financial Action Task Force (FATF) Recommendation 15, which addresses virtual assets and virtual asset service providers.

**Key provisions:**

1. **Reporting obligation for individuals:** Any resident individual conducting crypto transactions exceeding $5,000 in aggregate annual value must file a declaration.

2. **Reporting obligation for platforms:** All crypto-asset service providers operating in Paraguay must report user transaction data.

3. **What must be reported:**
   - Total annual transaction volume
   - Wallet addresses used
   - Counterparty identification (where available)
   - Type of crypto assets transacted
   - Date ranges of activity

4. **Timing:** Annual filing, due within 90 days after the close of the fiscal year.

### What Is NOT in the Resolution

Crucially, Resolution 47/2026 does NOT:

- **Impose a capital gains tax on crypto** — no mention of taxing gains
- **Create a wealth tax on crypto holdings** — no tax on total portfolio value
- **Change the territorial tax system** — foreign income remains untaxed
- **Introduce an exit tax** — leaving Paraguay has no tax consequence
- **Require reporting of every transaction** — only aggregated annual data
- **Apply retroactively** — only forward-looking from March 2026

## Why It's Not a Crypto Tax

This is the single most important distinction to understand.

### What a Tax Looks Like (Examples)

| Country | Crypto Tax | Rate |
|---------|-----------|------|
| Italy | Capital gains tax | 33% flat |
| Netherlands | Unrealised gains tax | 36% |
| Germany | Short-term income tax | Up to 47.5% |
| Spain | Savings income tax | Up to 28% |
| Australia | Capital gains tax | Up to 47% (with CGT discount) |

### What Paraguay Has

| Activity | Tax Rate |
|----------|---------|
| Foreign crypto trading gains | 0% |
| Foreign crypto staking yield | 0% |
| Foreign DeFi income | 0% |
| Foreign NFT sales | 0% |
| Crypto held as investment | 0% wealth tax |
| Crypto passed to heirs | 0% inheritance tax |
| **Annual reporting compliance** | **Required** |

The reporting requirement exists to combat money laundering and terrorist financing, not to collect tax revenue. Paraguay's territorial tax system has not changed. Foreign-source income — including crypto gains — remains at 0%.

## DNIT Res 47 vs. EU DAC8: A Critical Comparison

Both are reporting frameworks. But the end result is completely different.

| Aspect | EU DAC8 | Paraguay DNIT 47 |
|--------|---------|-------------------|
| **Effective date** | January 1, 2026 | March 2026 |
| **Reporting required** | Yes | Yes |
| **Transaction threshold** | €1,000+ | $5,000+ annual |
| **Wallet-level reporting** | Planned | Yes |
| **DeFi covered** | Not yet | Covered |
| **Data shared internationally** | Yes, all EU states | No (not CRS-compatible) |
| **Tax rate on crypto gains** | 28%-48% depending on country | 0% |
| **Tax on unrealised gains** | In Netherlands only (36%) | 0% |
| **Penalties for non-reporting** | Yes | Yes (administrative) |
| **Purpose** | Tax enforcement | AML/KYC compliance |

The critical difference: DAC8's purpose is tax collection. It enables EU tax authorities to assess and collect crypto gains taxes. DNIT Res 47's purpose is transparency. Paraguay already has 0% tax on foreign crypto gains — there's nothing to collect.

## What This Means for Crypto Investors

### The Compliance Burden

You must file an annual declaration. But compared to tax filings in most countries, the burden is light:

- Declare aggregate annual transaction volume
- List wallet addresses
- No need to calculate gains or losses
- No tax payment required
- File through a local accountant (~$200-$500/year)

### What You Should NOT Do

1. **Don't panic** — this is not a tax
2. **Don't hide** — reporting is mandatory; non-compliance carries penalties
3. **Don't assume** — if you have questions about your specific situation, consult a Paraguayan tax attorney

### What You Should Do

1. Maintain records of all crypto transactions
2. Keep exchange statements and wallet logs
3. Hire a local accountant for annual filing
4. Continue operating normally — your 0% tax rate hasn't changed

## The Strategic Advantage

DNIT Res 47/2026 actually creates a competitive advantage for Paraguay over other jurisdictions:

### Compared to EU Countries

In the EU, DAC8 reporting leads directly to tax bills. In Paraguay, reporting leads to... nothing. No tax due. This makes Paraguay the only jurisdiction where you can be fully compliant and pay 0%.

### Compared to UAE

The UAE doesn't have individual crypto reporting for residents. But the UAE also has no citizenship path, has CRS, and costs far more to enter. Paraguay's reporting requirement is a small price to pay for citizenship eligibility and CRS avoidance.

### Compared to Offshore Islands

The Cayman Islands, BVI, and Bahamas don't report either — but they also don't offer affordable entry, real citizenship paths, or the quality of life you can get in Paraguay for $1,200/month.

## Common Misconceptions — Busted

**"DNIT Res 47 means Paraguay is taxing crypto."**
False. It is a reporting resolution. No tax has been imposed on foreign crypto gains. The territorial tax system is unchanged.

**"I need to report every trade I make."**
No. Reporting is aggregated annual data, not per-transaction. You declare total volume, wallets, and crypto types.

**"My data will be shared with my home country."**
No. Paraguay does not participate in CRS. Your DNIT declaration stays in Paraguay.

**"Paraguay is becoming less crypto-friendly."**
False. Paraguay is becoming more regulated, not less friendly. Regulated environments attract legitimate business and banking relationships.

## The Bottom Line

DNIT Resolution 47/2026 introduces reporting obligations for crypto holders in Paraguay. It requires an annual declaration if your transaction volume exceeds $5,000. But it does not impose any tax on crypto gains, holdings, or transfers.

Paraguay remains the world's most attractive jurisdiction for crypto investors: 0% tax on foreign crypto gains, no CRS, citizenship in 3 years, and a clear, transparent regulatory framework. The reporting requirement is a small compliance step that actually strengthens the ecosystem by bringing it into the formal financial system.

Don't let sensational headlines confuse you. DNIT Res 47 is not a crypto tax. It's documentation that your crypto is moving through legitimate channels — so you can keep the 0% rate that makes Paraguay unique.

posts.title: Paraguay's Tax Environment: The Essentials Explained Simply
posts.excerpt: Territorial system, 10% tax rate, VAT, withholdings — what it means for you.
posts.author: Nexa Paraguay
posts.content:
## Introduction

Paraguay's tax system is the primary reason Europeans are looking at the country in 2026. But understanding how it actually works — not the marketing version, but the real mechanics — is essential before making a decision. This article explains the territorial system, the 10% rate, VAT, and what tax residency really means.

## The Territorial System

Paraguay operates a territorial (source-based) tax system. This means only income generated within Paraguayan territory is subject to Paraguayan taxation. Income earned outside Paraguay — foreign salary, overseas investments, rental income from properties abroad, foreign business profits — is not taxed in Paraguay.

This is the fundamental difference between Paraguay and nearly every European country, which tax worldwide income. If you are a Spanish tax resident, Spain taxes your global income. If you are a Paraguayan tax resident, Paraguay taxes only your Paraguayan-source income.

The key legal concept is "source." Income is considered Paraguayan-source if the activity producing it occurs in Paraguay. A remote worker employed by a Dutch company, working from Asunción, is generating foreign-source income — not taxable in Paraguay. A consulting project for a Paraguayan client, however, is Paraguayan-source income.

## The 10% IRE Rate

IRE (Impuesto a la Renta Empresarial) is the corporate income tax rate — 10%. This is a flat rate on net profits from Paraguayan-source business activities. It applies to both companies and individuals engaged in business activities. For individuals with only employment income, the rate is also 10% (IRP — Impuesto a la Renta del Personal).

Compare this to corporate tax rates in Europe: Germany (~30%), France (~25%), Netherlands (~25.8%), Spain (~25%). The difference compounds significantly over time.

## VAT (IVA)

Paraguay's VAT is called IVA (Impuesto al Valor Agregado). The standard rate is 10%, with a reduced rate of 5% for certain essential goods and services. Export services are zero-rated, meaning you can claim input VAT credits on related expenses.

For a foreign investor moving to Paraguay, IVA is largely invisible — it is embedded in the prices you pay for goods and services. The main impact is on businesses, which must register for IVA, issue tax receipts, and file monthly returns.

## Withholding Taxes

Dividends distributed by a Paraguayan company to its shareholders are subject to a 15% withholding tax if paid to foreign residents, and 5% if paid to a local individual. Interest payments to foreign lenders are generally subject to 15% withholding, though this may be reduced under applicable tax treaties.

Paraguay has a growing network of double taxation treaties, including agreements with Spain, Chile, Uruguay, and several other LATAM countries. However, there is no treaty with the Netherlands, Germany, or the UK — meaning treaty benefits are not available for most European investors.

## Filing and Compliance

Tax returns in Paraguay are filed annually, with monthly advance payments (anticipos) for established businesses. The tax year runs from January to December. Filing is done online through the SET portal (Marangatu). The system is fully digital, but the interface is in Spanish only.

For a new resident with only foreign income, the filing obligation is minimal — you file a zero or near-zero annual return declaring no Paraguayan-source income. This is straightforward but must be done correctly to maintain compliance.

## Common Misconceptions

**"I pay 0% as a foreigner."** Not exactly. You pay 0% on foreign income, but if you earn money from Paraguayan clients or operate a Paraguayan company, you pay the applicable rates.

**"I don't need to file taxes."** You do. Even with zero local income, you must file an annual declaration. Failure to file can result in fines and complications with residency renewal.

**"Territorial means no tax reporting at all."** Paraguay does not require you to declare foreign assets or income on your local return. However, if you are a tax resident, your country of origin may still require reporting under its own rules.

## How Nexa Paraguay Handles Tax Planning

Our tax team structures your affairs to optimize your position under Paraguayan law while maintaining compliance in your home country. We handle RUC registration, tax filings, and provide ongoing advisory for companies and individuals. We also coordinate with your home-country tax advisor to ensure cross-border compliance.

## Próximos pasos

If you are evaluating Paraguay seriously, the best way to move forward is a free 30-minute consultation. We do them in Dutch, English, German, or Spanish — no commitment.

**[Schedule a free consultation](/s/en/nexa-paraguay/contacto)**

posts.title: Leaving the EU cleanly: the paperwork nobody tells you about
posts.excerpt: Getting Paraguayan residency is the easy half. Unwinding your European tax ties is where investors get stuck. Here's the checklist by country.
posts.author: Nexa Paraguay
posts.content:
Every week we talk to a European investor who's already researched Paraguay, has their plan, and asks: "when can we start?" Our honest answer is usually: "you can start Paraguay today. But you can't finish Europe until next spring."

Getting Paraguayan residency is the well-defined half of the emigration. Unwinding your European tax ties is where the friction lives. This post is what the home-country side actually looks like by jurisdiction — enough to plan around, not enough to replace your local tax advisor.

## The universal rule

Paraguayan residency makes you a Paraguayan tax resident. It does **not** automatically make you stop being a tax resident somewhere else. Each European country has its own rules for breaking tax residency — and several of them actively tax the moment of departure.

Three categories of friction, in order of how much they cost investors:

1. **Exit taxes** — charged when you leave (Netherlands, Germany, some French structures)
2. **Continuing obligations** — carry on after you leave (UK deemed domicile, Belgian securities tax)
3. **Filing complexity** — not a cost, but a paperwork burden (Spain, Italy)

## Netherlands — the high-friction case

The Netherlands is the most complicated EU jurisdiction we regularly work with. Three specific items:

**Box 3 on worldwide wealth.** As long as you're NL-resident, box 3 taxes your global wealth on a fictitious return. It stops the day you break residency — but the Belastingdienst can challenge that date if ties remain.

**Emigratieheffing (exit tax on substantial interest).** If you own ≥5% of a BV (or equivalent), departure is treated as a deemed sale for capital gains purposes. You can **defer** the liability with the right structure (conservatoire assessment, bank guarantee), but you cannot escape it without triggering penalties.

**Woonplaatsverklaring van Emigratie.** The formal statement of emigration. Without it, the Belastingdienst presumes continued residency. With it, date certainty on the break.

**Practical sequencing we see work:**
- File intent to emigrate with the Belastingdienst 4 weeks before departure
- Obtain bank guarantee for emigratieheffing deferral (arrange in parallel)
- Break formal ties same week you fly: deregister from BRP, notify healthcare insurer, close non-essential local bank accounts
- File partial-year box 3 up to departure date with the following spring's return

**Budget:** EUR 2,000–5,000 in Dutch-side professional fees for clean emigration. Worth every euro.

## Germany — the exit-tax trap

Germany's Wegzugsteuer applies to substantial holdings (≥1% of a corporation). Unlike the Dutch case, the German rules for post-EU-exit destinations tightened in 2022 — Paraguay, not being in the EU/EEA, triggers immediate payment rather than deferral.

**What this means in practice:**
- If your main assets are a salaried role + portfolio of publicly-traded shares: clean exit, minimal tax impact.
- If you own ≥1% of a German GmbH or AG: Wegzugsteuer applies on the deemed capital gain. Deferral options are narrower than the Dutch case.
- If you hold investment assets in a German private bank: the bank's departure-customer process can take 6–8 weeks.

**Practical sequencing:** engage a German tax advisor (Steuerberater) 3–6 months before departure; consider intermediate EU jurisdiction if GmbH structure is large enough to warrant it; close tax year cleanly — emigration triggers a short-year return.

**Budget:** EUR 3,000–8,000 for tax advisor + any required valuations.

## Belgium — middle complexity

Below Germany's, above France's. Three notes:

- **Belgian securities transaction tax (TOB)** continues to apply to Belgian-resident investors for a wash-out period after departure. Not enormous but worth planning.
- **Tax on exit-year capital gains** on certain structures (SPA, SPRL equivalent stakes).
- **Registration at the commune** — Belgian emigration is declared at the municipal level, not just national tax authority.

**Budget:** EUR 1,500–3,000 Belgian-side.

## UK — the deemed-domicile question

For UK investors, the question isn't residency — you can break UK residency cleanly via the Statutory Residence Test (SRT). The question is **domicile**, a common-law concept that's stickier than tax residency.

- You can be non-UK-resident but still UK-domiciled for IHT purposes
- Domicile changes require demonstrated intent + severed ties + new domicile of choice (which Paraguay supports)
- Most investors get non-residency in the first full tax year after departure; domicile change takes 3–5 years of consistent evidence

**Budget:** GBP 2,000–6,000 UK tax advisor fees.

## Spain — simpler than most

Spain's regime is straightforward for most profiles: declare emigration to the Agencia Tributaria, last full-year Spanish return for the calendar year of departure, deregister at the Padrón. Most Spanish investors exit cleanly in 3–4 months.

**Budget:** EUR 800–2,000 for asesor fiscal fees.

## Italy — paperwork burden without the tax sting

Italy's regime for departing residents is mostly about filing. No exit tax on most profiles, but the AIRE registration (Italians abroad) + last-year return + tax-year close can take 6 months of back-and-forth.

**Budget:** EUR 1,000–3,000 for commercialista fees.

## What Nexa handles vs. what you need locally

**We handle:** Paraguayan residency + cédula, Paraguayan company incorporation, Paraguayan bank account, Paraguayan tax registration and first-year compliance.

**We coordinate with (but don't replace):** your home-country tax advisor for exit, your home-country bank for reference letter, your home-country notary/apostille authority.

**The mistake to avoid:** trying to handle the home-country exit yourself because "it's just paperwork." The structural fees are small; the tax cost of getting it wrong can be 30–40% of capital gains on your deemed-sale assets. Engage a local tax advisor.

## Parallel timeline

The two sides can run in parallel if you start early:

- **Month 0:** engage Nexa + engage home-country tax advisor
- **Month 1–2:** document collection on both sides
- **Month 3 (Paraguay):** operational day + residency filing
- **Month 4:** home-country emigration declaration (timed with Paraguayan cédula issuance for cleanest evidence)
- **Months 5–12:** tax-year close on home side, full Paraguayan integration

Done well, the total project is 8–12 months end-to-end when you need to break EU tax residency cleanly. The Paraguayan 8–12 weeks is just the middle slice.

**[Book a free consultation](/s/en/nexa-paraguay/contacto)** to map your specific exit. We'll flag the home-country items before you start, so nothing surprises you in month six.

posts.title: Paraguay vs Europe's Digital Nomad Visas: Less Income, Less Tax, Less Time
posts.excerpt: Europe's digital nomad visas sound appealing but hide high taxes and income requirements: Spain €32K+24% tax, Portugal €3,680/mo+up to 48%, Greece €42K/yr+7-22%. Paraguay requires $0 minimum income, charges 0% tax, and grants permanent residency — not just a visa.
posts.author: Nexa Paraguay
posts.content:
## The European Digital Nomad Visa Boom

Europe jumped on the digital nomad bandwagon in 2022-2024, with Spain, Portugal, Greece, Croatia, and others launching dedicated visa programs. On paper, they offer a path to live in Europe while working remotely.

**But the fine print tells a different story.** Minimum income requirements range from €2,100 to €42,000 per year, and taxes eat up 7% to 48% of your income. Plus, these are temporary visas — not paths to permanent residency or citizenship.

## Europe's Digital Nomad Visas — The Reality

### Spain Digital Nomad Visa

| Requirement | Detail |
|-------------|--------|
| Minimum income | **€32,040/year** (€2,670/month) |
| Tax rate | **24%** (for income <€600K under Beckham Law) |
| Duration | 1 year, renewable for up to 5 years |
| Path to residency | Yes (after 5 years) |
| Path to citizenship | After 10 years |
| Physical presence | 183 days/year |

The Spanish DNV requires you to prove significant income (nearly €2,700/month) and still pays **24% tax**. And the Beckham Law is not a given — it must be individually applied for.

### Portugal D8 Digital Nomad Visa

| Requirement | Detail |
|-------------|--------|
| Minimum income | **€3,680/month** (4x minimum wage) |
| Tax rate | **20%** (flat under NHR-friendly regime) **up to 48%** (standard) |
| Duration | 1 year, renewable |
| Path to residency | 5 years |
| Path to citizenship | 5-6 years |
| Physical presence | 183 days/year |

Portugal's D8 visa hits you with at least 20% tax, potentially rising to 48% if you don't qualify for favorable regimes. And the NHR scheme that made Portugal famous? **Dead since 2025.**

### Greece Digital Nomad Visa

| Requirement | Detail |
|-------------|--------|
| Minimum income | **€42,000/year** (€3,500/month) |
| Tax rate | **7-22%** (first 7 years, if non-EU resident) |
| Duration | 1 year, renewable |
| Path to residency | Yes |
| Path to citizenship | 7 years |
| Physical presence | 183 days/year |

Greece requires the **highest minimum income** of all — €42,000/year. While the tax rate of 7-22% is attractive for the first 7 years, you're still tied to the 183-day rule and a 7-year path to citizenship.

### Croatia Digital Nomad Visa

| Requirement | Detail |
|-------------|--------|
| Minimum income | **€2,500/month** (€30,000/year) |
| Tax rate | **20%** (lump sum option, otherwise standard rates) |
| Duration | 1 year (non-renewable) |
| Path to residency | **None** (no path to permanent residency) |
| Path to citizenship | None |
| Physical presence | Required |

Croatia's visa is arguably the most limited: it's **not renewable** and offers **no path to permanent residency or citizenship**. You get one year, and then you're out.

## The Paraguay Alternative

### Paraguay's Residency Program

| Requirement | Detail |
|-------------|--------|
| Minimum income | **$0** — no income requirement |
| Tax rate | **0%** on all foreign-source income |
| Status | **Permanent residency** (not a visa) |
| Duration to permanent residency | **1 year** |
| Path to citizenship | **3 years** |
| Physical presence to maintain | **1 visit every 3 years** |

**No income minimum, no tax, permanent residency, citizenship in 3 years. Europe can't compete.**

## Direct Comparison

### By the Numbers

| Program | Min. Income | Tax Rate | Physical Presence | Permanent Residency | Citizenship |
|---------|-------------|----------|-------------------|-------------------|-------------|
| **Paraguay** | **$0** | **0%** | **1 visit/3yr** | **1 year** | **3 years** |
| Spain DNV | €32K/yr | 24% | 183 days/yr | 5 years | 10 years |
| Portugal D8 | €3,680/mo | 20-48% | 183 days/yr | 5 years | 5-6 years |
| Greece DNV | €42K/yr | 7-22% | 183 days/yr | 5 years | 7 years |
| Croatia DNV | €2,500/mo | 20% | Required | **None** | None |

### The Tax Impact: Real World Example

Imagine a digital nomad earning **$80,000/year** from US or EU clients:

| Destination | Tax on $80K | Net Income | Rent | Disposable |
|-------------|-------------|------------|------|-----------|
| **Paraguay** | **$0** | **$80,000** | **$4,800/yr** | **$75,200** |
| Spain (24%) | $19,200 | $60,800 | $16,800/yr | $44,000 |
| Portugal (20%) | $16,000 | $64,000 | $13,200/yr | $50,800 |
| Greece (7%) * | $5,600 | $74,400 | $14,400/yr | $60,000 |
| Croatia (20%) | $16,000 | $64,000 | $10,800/yr | $53,200 |

*\*Greece's 7% rate is first-year only — rises to 22%*

**Paraguay leaves you with $14,400 to $31,200 more per year than any European DNV program.**

## Beyond the Numbers: Why Permanent Residency Matters

European digital nomad visas share a critical weakness: **they are temporary by design.**

- **Spain DNV:** 1 year, renewable up to 5 years, then you must apply for residency
- **Portugal D8:** 1 year renewable, residency after 5 years
- **Croatia:** 1 year, **not renewable**, no path to residency
- **Paraguay:** You get **permanent residency** after 1 year. Citizenship after 3 years.

This isn't just about today's tax bill — it's about long-term security. A temporary visa can be revoked, changed, or made more expensive. Permanent residency gives you stability.

## The Hidden Costs of European Visas

### 1. Banking Restrictions
As a DNV holder in Europe, you'll often face non-resident banking fees, difficulty opening accounts, and limited credit options.

### 2. Healthcare
European DNVs usually require private health insurance (€50-150/month) without access to public systems. Paraguay's private insurance costs €35-100/month with immediate access to top clinics.

### 3. Tax Compliance
Europe's tax systems are complex. You'll likely need a tax advisor (€1,000-3,000/year) to navigate double taxation treaties, social security, and local filings.

### 4. Catching Up with Inflation
As European countries raise minimum wage requirements for DNV renewals, you must demonstrate growing income. In Paraguay, there's no income requirement to maintain.

## Who Should Choose Which?

### Choose Paraguay if:
- You earn more than €30K/year and want to keep it
- You value long-term residency over a temporary visa
- You don't want to be tied to 183 days/year in one country
- Citizenship in 3 years appeals to you
- You're willing to invest in learning Spanish

### Choose Europe if:
- You need to stay within Europe for family or business reasons
- You earn under €30K/year (but then minimum income requirements hurt)
- You only want a 1-2 year adventure, not permanent relocation
- You prefer European infrastructure and proximity to home

## The Verdict

Europe's digital nomad visas are **expensive, temporary, and tax-heavy**. Paraguay offers a **permanent solution** with zero tax, no income requirements, and citizenship in 3 years.

**The only real advantage Europe has is proximity to home. But with Paraguay's tax savings, you can afford to fly back business class multiple times a year.**

### Ready to Compare?

- **Post-residency services** — Banking, tax setup, community integration

**Your $0 tax life starts here. Book your free call today.**

posts.title: Why Paraguay Is the Best Country for FIRE Retirees in 2026
posts.excerpt: With a $500K FIRE portfolio producing $20K/year at the 4% rule, Paraguay offers a comfortable lifestyle that most countries can't match. No tax on withdrawals, $1,100-1,500/month living costs, and citizenship in 3 years — compare to Costa Rica, Portugal, Thailand, and Panama.
posts.author: Nexa Paraguay
posts.content:
## FIRE in Paraguay: The Math That Changes Everything

The FIRE movement is built on a simple equation: save enough that your portfolio can sustain your lifestyle indefinitely. The 4% rule says you can withdraw 4% of your portfolio annually, adjusted for inflation, and never run out of money.

In many countries, a $500K portfolio generating $20K/year ($1,667/month) barely covers rent. In Paraguay, it funds a lifestyle that would cost $5,000-6,000/month in the US.

Here's why Paraguay is the best FIRE destination in 2026.

## The Core FIRE Numbers

| FIRE Portfolio | 4% Annual Withdrawal | Monthly Budget | Lifestyle in PY |
|---------------|---------------------|----------------|-----------------|
| $250,000 | $10,000 | $833 | Basic, shared housing |
| $500,000 | $20,000 | $1,667 | Very comfortable (sweet spot) |
| $750,000 | $30,000 | $2,500 | Premium lifestyle, travel |
| $1,000,000 | $40,000 | $3,333 | Luxury, frequent travel |
| $1,500,000 | $60,000 | $5,000 | Top-tier luxury |

**The sweet spot:** $500,000. At $1,667/month, you live extremely well in Paraguay — modern 2-bedroom apartment, dining out regularly, gym membership, and international travel twice a year.

## Tax: The FIRE Killer

The single biggest expense for most FIRE retirees is taxes. In almost every country, your investment withdrawals are taxed as income. Paraguay's territorial tax system means:

- **0% tax on capital gains** from foreign investments
- **0% tax on dividends** from foreign shares
- **0% tax on interest** from foreign accounts
- **0% tax on crypto profits** (crypto is classified as goods, not securities)
- **No wealth tax**
- **No inheritance tax**

Compare this to:

| Country | Tax on Investment Withdrawals | Wealth Tax | Effective Tax Rate on $20K PY Withdrawal |
|---------|------------------------------|------------|----------------------------------------|
| **Paraguay** | 0% | 0% | **0%** |
| USA | 0-20% + state tax + NIIT | 0% | 0-35% depending on state |
| Portugal (NHR 2.0) | Flat 10% or 28% | 0% | 10-28% |
| Costa Rica | 0% (territorial) | 0% | 0% |
| Thailand | 0-35% if remitted in year of earning | 0% | 0-35% |
| Panama | 0% (territorial) | 0% | 0% |
| Spain | 19-26% (savings rate) | 0.2-3.5% | 19-26%+ |
| UAE | 0% | 0% | 0% |

**Paraguay ties with Panama, UAE, and Costa Rica for tax — but beats them on cost and citizenship path.**

## Cost of Living Comparison

| Category | Paraguay | Costa Rica | Portugal | Thailand | Panama |
|----------|----------|-----------|---------|---------|--------|
| Monthly budget (comfortable) | $1,100-1,500 | $2,000-3,000 | $2,000-3,000 | $1,200-2,000 | $1,800-2,500 |
| Rent (1BR, city center) | $350-500 | $600-900 | $800-1,200 | $400-600 | $700-1,000 |
| Rent (2BR, city center) | $500-800 | $900-1,300 | $1,200-1,800 | $600-900 | $1,000-1,500 |
| Meal, inexpensive restaurant | $5-7 | $8-12 | $10-15 | $3-5 | $8-12 |
| Domestic beer | $1-2 | $2-3 | $2-3 | $1.50-2.50 | $1.50-2.50 |
| Utilities (monthly) | $60-100 | $80-120 | $100-150 | $70-100 | $80-120 |
| Internet | $25-40 | $40-60 | $35-50 | $20-30 | $30-50 |
| Gym membership | $20-40 | $40-60 | $30-50 | $25-40 | $35-60 |
| Monthly healthcare | $35-80 | $80-150 | $50-100 | $50-80 | $80-150 |

## Citizenship Path Comparison

For FIRE retirees, citizenship matters. You want the security of a second passport without a massive investment.

| Country | Citizenship Timeline | Minimum Investment | Physical Presence Required | Dual Citizenship Allowed |
|---------|---------------------|-------------------|---------------------------|-------------------------|
| **Paraguay** | **3 years** | **$0 (nominal fees)** | **0 days/year** | **Yes** |
| Panama | 5-8 years | $300K+ (Friendly Nations visa) | 1 day/2 years | Yes |
| Portugal | 5 years | None (D7 visa) | 183 days/year | Yes |
| Spain | 10 years | None (non-lucrative visa) | 183 days/year | Partial (must renounce EU citizenship) |
| Uruguay | 3-5 years | $180K+ investment | 183 days/year | Yes |
| Costa Rica | 7 years | None (rentista) | 183 days/year | Yes |
| Thailand | No citizenship path | N/A | N/A | N/A |
| UAE | No citizenship path | N/A | N/A | N/A |

**Paraguay wins decisively:** 3 years to citizenship, zero investment, zero physical presence requirement.

## FIRE Scenario Comparison: $500K Portfolio

Let's see what a $500K portfolio ($20K/year at 4%) buys in different countries:

| Destination | Monthly Budget | Housing | Lifestyle | Tax on Withdrawals | Can You Actually Retire? |
|-------------|---------------|---------|-----------|-------------------|-------------------------|
| **Paraguay** | $1,667 | 2BR modern apt ($500) | Comfortable, dining out, travel | $0 | **Yes** |
| Costa Rica | $1,667 | 1BR basic ($700) | Tight budget | $0 | Tight |
| Portugal | $1,667 | Room/shared ($600) | Very tight | $167/mo | No |
| Thailand | $1,667 | 1BR nice ($450) | Comfortable | $0 (if not remitted) | Yes (but no citizenship) |
| Panama | $1,667 | Studio ($600) | Tight | $0 | Tight |
| Spain | $1,667 | Room ($500) | Very tight | $317/mo | No |
| USA (MCOL) | $1,667 | Room ($800) | Bare minimum | $0-200 | No |

## The FIRE Scorecard

| Factor | Paraguay Score | Notes |
|--------|---------------|-------|
| Cost of Living | A+ | Cheapest safe option for Western retirees |
| Tax on Withdrawals | A+ | 0% on all foreign capital gains |
| Citizenship Speed | A+ | 3 years — fastest in South America |
| Healthcare Quality | B+ | Good private care, $50-150/mo insurance |
| Safety | B+ | Low violent crime in expat areas |
| English Ease | B- | Spanish helpful but not required |
| Internet Quality | A- | Fiber available, 100-300 Mbps |
| Expat Community | B | Growing but not saturated |
| Travel Access | B | South America hub, good regional flights |

## The $500K FIRE Budget Breakdown in Paraguay

| Category | Monthly Cost | Notes |
|----------|-------------|-------|
| Rent (2BR, Villa Morra) | $500 | Modern apartment, pool, gym |
| Electricity, water, gas | $80 | AC in summer adds $30-40 |
| Internet (fiber) | $35 | 200 Mbps |
| Groceries | $250 | Fresh produce, meat, imports |
| Dining out (8-10x/month) | $200 | Casual restaurants, street food |
| Gym membership | $30 | Premium gym |
| Healthcare insurance | $75 | Private international plan |
| Transportation | $60 | Uber/Bolt + occasional bus |
| Entertainment + hobbies | $150 | Movies, sports, events |
| Travel fund | $150 | Regional trips |
| Miscellaneous | $137 | Phone, clothes, incidentals |
| **Total** | **$1,667** | **All-in** |

## Why Paraguay Over Each Competitor

### Paraguay vs Portugal

Portugal's NHR regime is dead. NHR 2.0 offers a flat 10% tax (not 0%), requires 183 days/year presence, and costs 2x more to live. Citizenship takes the same 5 years but requires actual residence.

### Paraguay vs Costa Rica

Costa Rica matches Paraguay on tax (0% foreign income) but costs nearly double to live and takes 7 years for citizenship with a 183-day presence requirement.

### Paraguay vs Thailand

Thailand has no path to citizenship. The Elite visa costs $18K-$143K with no permanence. Tax on remitted foreign income is 0-35% and recently tightened. You're always a guest, never a citizen.

### Paraguay vs Panama

Panama is 30-50% more expensive, takes 5-8 years for citizenship, and requires minimum $300K investment for the Friendly Nations visa.

## The Bottom Line

For FIRE retirees in 2026, Paraguay is the clear winner:

- **$500K portfolio is enough** for a very comfortable life
- **0% tax on all withdrawals** — your money goes further
- **$1,100-1,500/month** covers everything
- **Citizenship in 3 years** — real permanence, not just a visa
- **No minimum physical presence** — travel freely

**Paraguay makes FIRE work on a budget that fails elsewhere.**

posts.title: The Difference Between a Gestoría and a Professional Team
posts.excerpt: An administrative facilitator is not the same as an integrated system with relational capital.
posts.author: Nexa Paraguay
posts.content:
## Introduction

If you have researched Paraguayan relocation services, you have encountered the word "gestoría." It sounds like a professional service. In practice, a gestoría is something more limited — and understanding the difference is critical to choosing the right support for your move.

## What Is a Gestoría?

A gestoría (from "gestor" — manager or facilitator) is essentially a document-running service. A gestor knows the physical locations of government offices, the opening hours, which window number to approach, and which forms to fill. Their core value is logistical: they save you from standing in line at Migraciones, the police records office, or the tax authority.

Gestores are individuals or small shops that operate on relationships with lower-level administrative staff. They know the clerk who processes residency applications, or the notary who can squeeze you in without an appointment. This is genuinely useful — navigating Paraguay's bureaucracy without local knowledge is frustrating and slow.

However, a gestoría has significant limits. A gestor is not a lawyer. They cannot provide legal advice, draft corporate bylaws, structure a tax plan, or review a real estate purchase contract. They are facilitators, not advisors.

## What a Multidisciplinary Team Provides

A professional team like Nexa Paraguay includes lawyers, accountants, sworn translators, notaries, and client managers working together. This is not a one-person operation with a network of subcontractors. It is an integrated system where each professional handles their domain:

- **Lawyers** handle corporate incorporation, residency applications, contract review, and legal due diligence on property
- **Accountants** manage RUC registration, tax filings, ongoing compliance, and financial planning
- **Sworn translators** handle all document translations with official registration at the Corte Suprema
- **Client managers** coordinate the logistics, timeline, and communication across all domains

The gestor runs documents. The professional team designs and executes strategy.

## Why Relational Capital Matters

The most important difference is relational capital at the decision-making level. A gestor knows the clerk. A professional firm has relationships with the bank compliance officer, the senior examiner at Migraciones, the notary who handles complex international transactions.

When a problem arises — a document is rejected, a bank application is flagged, a registry deadline is missed — the gestor escalates to the same clerk. The professional firm makes a phone call to someone who can resolve the issue with a decision. This is not about "shortcuts" or corruption. It is about working with people who have the authority and expertise to solve problems, not just process paperwork.

## Cost Comparison

A gestoría typically charges $200–$500 per procedure. For a full residency application, a gestor might charge $1,000–$2,000. A professional team charges $3,000–$5,000 for the full package including residency, company incorporation, RUC, and bank account setup.

The gestor is cheaper on paper. But consider what you get for the additional investment: legal review of your documents, tax structure design, post-approval support, and — most importantly — someone who can fix things when they go wrong. The gestor hands you the completed form and moves on. The professional team stays with you through the entire process and beyond.

## When Each Makes Sense

A gestoría is appropriate for simple, routine procedures: renewing a driver's license, obtaining a duplicate ID card, filing a straightforward tax return for a long-term resident who already knows the system.

For complex, high-stakes procedures — first-time residency applications, corporate incorporation with foreign shareholders, property purchases requiring title due diligence, tax planning for international income — a professional team is the appropriate choice. The cost difference is modest compared to the consequences of errors.

## Common Mistakes

The most frequent mistake is hiring a gestor for a residency application, then discovering midway that you need legal advice on document legalization, or that the gestor cannot open a bank account for you because they lack the relationship with compliance. You end up paying twice — once for the gestor, then for a professional team to fix what went wrong.

Another mistake is assuming all "lawyers" are the same. Many solo practitioners in Paraguay operate more as gestores than as attorneys. Ask your provider: who specifically will review my documents? Who will handle the bank introductions? Who will be responsible if my residency application is denied?

## How Nexa Paraguay Differentiates

We are a multidisciplinary firm, not a gestoría. Our team includes lawyers registered with the Paraguayan Bar Association, accountants registered with the SET as tax advisors, and sworn translators registered with the Corte Suprema. Every client has a dedicated manager who coordinates across all domains and reports progress weekly.

If you are evaluating Paraguay seriously, the best way to move forward is a free 30-minute consultation. We do them in Dutch, English, German, or Spanish — no commitment.
